explanations.explanation: Micah comes right out with it. He tells his mother, "…I have the silver here with me; I took it." (Judges 17:2) He had heard her utter a curse about that silver, and he owns up anyway. That's a man who walks up to the oven and says, "I'm the one who ate the dough."

Actually, Micah is the one who took it. He says to his mother, "…I have the silver here with me; I took it." (Judges 17:2) So there's no mystery thief to hunt down. The culprit is standing right there talking to her.

explanations.answer: Blessed be my son by the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's what she says: "Blessed be my son by the LORD!" (Judges 17:2) Picture it. Her silver is gone, Micah says he heard her utter a curse about it, and then her own boy says he took it. I would have expected a very different speech, friend.

explanations.answer: Shame on my son before the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's a natural guess, friend. But she doesn't say shame. She says, "Blessed be my son by the LORD!" (Judges 17:2) Her words aren't what I'd have seen coming at all.

explanations.answer: My son has brought a curse on us
explanations.explanation: That's a fair guess, since Micah had heard her utter a curse about the silver. But what she says is, "Blessed be my son by the LORD!" (Judges 17:2) A curse about the silver, and then a blessing for her son. I'd be checking my own ears twice, friend.

explanations.answer: A graven image and a molten idol
explanations.explanation: She says she wholly dedicates the silver to the LORD to make "…a graven image and a molten idol." (Judges 17:3) Those are the two things she names. I'll just say this plainly, friend: it's a heavy thing to see an image come out of silver she said was for the LORD.

explanations.answer: A gold lampstand for the tabernacle
explanations.explanation: That one belongs to a different story. The text says nothing about a lampstand or the tabernacle here. She says she'll use the silver "…to make a graven image and a molten idol." (Judges 17:3)
Not an altar this time. The silver is for "…a graven image and a molten idol." (Judges 17:3) Bronze isn't even in the picture, since this is all silver.

Yes, the graven image and molten idol "…were placed in the house of Micah." (Judges 17:4) Two hundred shekels of silver went to a silversmith, and the finished pieces ended up under Micah's roof. That's quite a trip for some silver, friend.
Not a field. The verse says they "…were placed in the house of Micah." (Judges 17:4) These weren't set out under the sky. They were put indoors.
No vineyard here, friend. The text says they "…were placed in the house of Micah." (Judges 17:4) The vines never get a mention at all.

That's right, Micah "…ordained one of his sons as his priest." (Judges 17:5) He keeps the priest job inside his own family. The verse says he had a shrine and made an ephod and some household idols, and then he picked a son for the job.
No servants in this verse. Micah "…ordained one of his sons as his priest." (Judges 17:5) The priest comes from his own children.

No brothers in this verse, friend. Micah "…ordained one of his sons as his priest." (Judges 17:5) When Micah needed a priest, he looked to his own boys. I think the brothers are still waiting by the phone for that call.

Right, the writer says, "everyone did what was right in his own eyes." (Judges 17:6) With no king, nobody is named as the one who decides for everybody. Picture a bakery with no head baker and everyone writing their own recipe. I did say picture it, friend.
The verse never says that. It says "everyone did what was right in his own eyes." (Judges 17:6) No priests are named as the ones deciding for the whole land.

explanations.answer: The elders decide for each town
explanations.explanation: That's not what the writer tells us. He says, "everyone did what was right in his own eyes." (Judges 17:6) Elders aren't mentioned in that line at all.

The text doesn't say anyone sent for him. It says the Levite "…left the city of Bethlehem in Judah to settle where he could find a place." (Judges 17:8) He was the one on the move, and he ended up at Micah's house along the way.

That's right. The young Levite "…left the city of Bethlehem in Judah to settle where he could find a place." (Judges 17:8) The text gives his own reason for leaving, and it isn't a message from Micah. He came to Micah's house as he traveled.

explanations.answer: Ten shekels a year plus clothes and provisions
explanations.explanation: That's the offer: "…ten shekels of silver per year, a suit of clothes, and your provisions." (Judges 17:10) Micah asks him to "…be my father and priest…" Ten silver shekels, a suit and his provisions, and the young man goes in and agrees to stay.

explanations.answer: Two hundred shekels and a house of his own
explanations.explanation: The two hundred shekels went to the silversmith, remember? Micah's offer to the Levite was "…ten shekels of silver per year, a suit of clothes, and your provisions." (Judges 17:10) No house of his own is on the list.

explanations.answer: A field and a share of the flocks
explanations.explanation: Micah doesn't offer land or flocks. He says, "…I will give you ten shekels of silver per year, a suit of clothes, and your provisions." (Judges 17:10) That's the whole package.
Yes, "…the young man became like a son to Micah." (Judges 17:11) Micah had asked him to be his father and priest. Now the Levite is treated like family under that roof.
Close, but the text says "…the young man became like a son to Micah." (Judges 17:11) Look at the flip, friend. Micah asked him to be his father, and he became like a son. A brother doesn't come up.
No, the Levite isn't called a master. The verse says "…the young man became like a son to Micah." (Judges 17:11) Micah is the one offering the pay, after all.

That's right: "Micah ordained the Levite, and the young man became his priest and lived in his house." (Judges 17:12) Earlier, Micah ordained one of his own sons. Now the Levite is the priest, and he's living right there in the house.

This one is true, friend. The verse says, "Micah ordained the Levite, and the young man became his priest and lived in his house." (Judges 17:12) So the Levite is Micah's priest, and he lives at Micah's place.

explanations.answer: Because a Levite has become his priest
explanations.explanation: That's his reason. Micah says, "Now I know that the LORD will be good to me, because a Levite has become my priest." (Judges 17:13) He's sure because of the Levite. I'll say it gently, friend: I think Micah is leaning hard on that one fact.

explanations.answer: Because his mother blessed him by the LORD
explanations.explanation: His mother did say, "Blessed be my son by the LORD!" (Judges 17:2) But that's not what Micah points to here. He says, "…because a Levite has become my priest." (Judges 17:13)

explanations.answer: Because the silver went back to his mother
explanations.explanation: The silver did go back to his mother (Judges 17:3-4), but Micah doesn't name that as his reason. He says, "Now I know that the LORD will be good to me, because a Levite has become my priest." (Judges 17:13) The Levite is the whole reason he gives.
